name: Tasmanian, North Midlands
confidence_why: Crowley and Dixon 1981, the standard reference sketch, call stress placement the most elusive part of Tasmanian phonology and conclude only that disyllables were stressed initially and any non-final syllable could bear stress, Capell 1968 likewise finds stress statements nearly impossible for a language known only from amateur wordlists and a few cylinder recordings, and the sole dissent, Taylor 2006's master's-thesis claim of initial stress read off Walker's and Robinson's diacritics, rests on the same marks Crowley and Dixon judged ambiguous between accent and length, so the undetermined record stands with few sources and one weaker contradiction.
catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry & R.M.W. Dixon. 1981. 'Tasmanian'. In R.M.W. Dixon & B.J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages, vol. 2, 394-421. Canberra: ANU Press / Amsterdam: John Benjamins. Open scan: ANU Open Research hdl:1885/114846.
catalog_locator: Section 2.4 'Stress', p. 413. Scope note: section 2.1, p. 407. Language inventory: section 1.4, pp. 402-403.
catalog_quote: The position of stress within a word is perhaps the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology. We have the following source material: [a] Walker marks each vowel with either ¯ or ˘; these marks apparently indicate accent rather than quantity (see the comment in Roth 1899, p.1 of Appendix). [b] Norman uses the same marks, probably in the same way. [c] Milligan says 'when a double consonant or two consonants stand together, the first carries the accent, as in the English words cunningly, peppery, cobbler, pipkin.' This somewhat elusive statement perhaps means that the vowel preceding a sequence of two consonants (in Milligan's orthography) bears stress. [d] Tindale's transcriptions. [e] The Fanny Cochrane Smith recordings. [f] The 1972 Crowley recordings of Mrs. Heffernan and Mrs. Mundy. From these sources it appears that a disyllabic word is always stressed on the first syllable, whereas a trisyllabic word can be stressed on either first or second syllable. Our only general conclusion concerning stress in Tasmanian is thus: any syllable except the last can bear stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Tasmanian languages collectively (reconstructed from 19th-c. spellings with stress diacritics and from early recordings): disyllables carry initial stress; trisyllables carry stress on the first or the second syllable; the only generalisation the authors commit to is that stress is never word-final. No positional rule specific to North Midlands is given, and none of the six evidence sources listed is North Midlands material.
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllables vary between first- and second-syllable stress; authors explicitly decline a firmer rule. Taylor 2006 (MA thesis, pp. 257-259) disputes their reading of the diacritics and argues the first word element was strongly stressed (initial prominence).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms in wordlists and a few recorded utterances; statement is pan-Tasmanian ('Tasmanian'), not variety-specific.
new_statements.identity_note: The only positional statements found (Crowley & Dixon 1981 p. 413; Taylor 2006 pp. 257-259; Capell 1968 p. 2) are about the Tasmanian languages collectively (Glottolog family-level tasm1247 bookkeeping / North-Eastern Tasmanian family for neta1235), reconstructed from 19th-century spellings. Crowley & Dixon's six stress evidence sources (Walker, Norman, Milligan, Tindale, Fanny Cochrane Smith cylinders, Crowley 1972 recordings) are all eastern/south-eastern or Bass Strait descendant material; none is North Midlands (AIATSIS T4, Tyerrernotepanner) or Northern (T1) vocabulary. Glottolog neta1235 = ISO xph; per ISO CR 2019-047 Glottolog's languoid conflates T4 North Midlands with T1 Northern, and Bowern 2012 did not separate North Midlands from Northeastern (nort3274-type cluster; Glottolog benl1235 for Ben Lomond/NE). A sibling folder already holds the same HAL vol. 2 scan and quotes the same passage for the family-level key.

sources.note: Pan-Tasmanian reconstruction from spellings and recordings: stress position 'the most elusive aspect'; evidence = Walker's and Norman's diacritics, Milligan's accent remark, Tindale's transcriptions, Fanny Cochrane Smith cylinders, Crowley's 1972 recordings (none of these is North Midlands material); disyllables always initial-stressed, trisyllables stressed on 1st or 2nd; only general conclusion 'any syllable except the last can bear stress'.

sources.citation: Taylor, John Albert. 2006. The Palawa (Tasmanian Aboriginal) languages: a preliminary discussion. MA thesis, University of Tasmania. Section 7.9 'Stress and Accenting', pp. 257-259; section 7.3.3 p. 138; section 6.1.13 p. 103 (Robinson's stress marks).
sources.note: Disagrees with Crowley & Dixon; from the bar/breve diacritics of Robinson, Sterling, Walker etc.: 'in 99 per cent of word elements in initial position with vowels bearing these diacritics, the first vowel is marked with a bar' -> 'completely consistent with strong stressing of the first word element in words'; applies Dixon's 'initial syllable is generally stressed' to Palawa but denies alternating rhythm. Pan-Palawa, no North Midlands-specific statement.

sources.citation: Milligan, Joseph. 1859. On the dialects and language of the Aboriginal Tribes of Tasmania.. Papers and Proceedings of the Royal Society of Tasmania 3(2): 275-282 (orthography/accent remark p. 282).
sources.note: Orthographic key only: 'When a double consonant, or two consonants stand together, the first carries the accent, as in the English words cunningly, peppery, cobbler, pipkin.' His vocabularies are Oyster Bay, Bruny/South-East and 'North-west', not North Midlands.
sources.venue: Papers and Proceedings of the Royal Society of Tasmania

sources.note: Nothing on stress, accent or prosody; lexical phylogenetics only. Places 'north midlands' vocabularies in the northeastern cluster. PDF not retrievable (EPMC render 403, PMC captcha); text read via direct download.

sources.note: 'In Tasmanian it is extremely hard to make statements about syllable structure or stress, because it is not possible to listen to living speakers. Something may be gained here from a study of song rhythms. Schmidt devotes a section (pp. 114-121) to syllabification and accent.' No positional rule given.
